message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Feasibility Study: Robotic Palletising on Lines 1 and 2
Operations Engineering, Kestrel Foods, Wrexley Plant, February 2026

1. Purpose
This study assesses whether to replace manual palletising at the end of packing Lines 1 and 2 with two robotic palletising cells, and recommends a course of action to the Plant Investment Board.

2. Current operation
Lines 1 and 2 pack savoury snacks into cases, which are stacked onto pallets by hand at the end of each line. Each line has two palletising operators per shift, and the lines run two shifts a day (06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00), five days a week. That is eight operator posts in total. At a fully loaded cost of £36,500 per operator per year, manual palletising costs £292,000 a year.

Palletising is the most physically demanding task on site. Operators lift around 4,000 cases per shift, and the task accounts for most of our manual-handling injuries.

Under the site plan agreed by the Board in December 2025, Lines 1 and 2 will move to a single day shift from January 2027, as volume consolidates onto the new high-speed Line 5.

3. The proposed solution
Each cell consists of a four-axis robot, a layer-forming conveyor, a pallet dispenser, safety guarding and a stretch-wrapper. One operator per shift would supervise both cells, handle pallet changes and clear faults.

Vendor trial
The preferred vendor ran a three-day trial in January using our actual cases and pallet patterns.

Table 1. Vendor trial results, 12-14 January 2026
Case type | Share of Line 1 and 2 volume | Peak rate (cases/min) | Sustained rate over 8 hours (cases/min)
14 kg catering case | 60% | 13 | 10.5
8 kg retail case | 40% | 16 | 14.0

Our lines run at up to 12 cases per minute. The trial confirmed that the cell sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types, comfortably above our line rate, so the cell will not become a bottleneck.

4. Safety benefit
Line 3 has had an automated case packer and palletiser since 2023. In 2025 it recorded 4 manual-handling injuries, compared with 11 across Lines 1 and 2. Automation clearly reduces injuries, and we expect robotic palletising to cut manual-handling injuries on Lines 1 and 2 by a similar proportion. For context, Line 3 runs the lighter 6 kg multipack cases and operates on a single shift.

5. Costs and savings
Table 2. Financial summary
Item | Amount
Capital: two cells, installed, including guarding and conveyors | £620,000
Annual maintenance contract (two cells) | £36,000
Remaining supervision: one operator per shift, two shifts | £73,000 per year
Current manual palletising cost | £292,000 per year
Net annual saving (£292,000 - £73,000 - £36,000) | £183,000
Simple payback (£620,000 / £183,000) | 3.4 years

The Plant Investment Board's hurdle for automation projects is a payback of four years or less, so the project meets the hurdle with a margin. The three operators displaced on each shift would be offered redeployment to Line 5, which is currently recruiting.

6. Implementation
The vendor quotes a 16-week lead time. Installation would take place during the planned two-week August shutdown, with a further two weeks of commissioning at reduced line speed. We would train two engineering technicians on robot maintenance as part of the contract.

7. Risks
Changeovers to new case sizes require reprogramming, which the vendor will provide for the first year. Pallet quality varies between suppliers, and poor pallets cause faults in automated dispensing; we will tighten our pallet specification before go-live.

8. Recommendation
Robotic palletising on Lines 1 and 2 is technically proven on our own products, removes our most injurious manual task and pays back in 3.4 years, within the Board's four-year hurdle. We recommend the Board approve capital of £620,000 for installation in the August 2026 shutdown.
</document>
response:
# Review: Robotic Palletising Feasibility Study, Lines 1 and 2

**Summary:** The arithmetic checks out, but two problems undermine the recommendation. The financial case ignores the move to single-shift operation that the document itself mentions, and the trial data contradicts the claim that the cell keeps up with the line. As written, the study shouldn't go to the Board.

## Critical issues

### 1. The savings assume two shifts, but the lines go to one shift in January 2027
Section 2 says Lines 1 and 2 move to a single day shift from January 2027, only about five months after the proposed August 2026 install. Section 5 still calculates savings on two shifts for the life of the asset.

On a single shift:

| Item | Two shifts (as written) | Single shift (from Jan 2027) |
|---|---|---|
| Manual palletising avoided (4 posts vs 8) | £292,000 | £146,000 |
| Remaining supervision (1 operator) | −£73,000 | −£36,500 |
| Maintenance | −£36,000 | −£36,000 |
| **Net annual saving** | **£183,000** | **£73,500** |
| **Simple payback** | **3.4 years** | **≈8.4 years** |

From 2027 onward, the project fails the Board's four-year hurdle by a wide margin. The few months of two-shift running before January don't change this materially. This needs to be the headline of the financial section, not left out.

### 2. The trial shows the cell can't keep up on the main product
Section 3 says the cell "sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types." Table 1 shows otherwise:
- The **14 kg catering case sustains 10.5 cases/min**, below the 12 cases/min line rate. That case is **60% of volume**.
- Even blended across the mix, the effective rate is about 11.7 cases/min (0.6/10.5 + 0.4/14 ≈ 0.086 min per case), still under 12.
- Only the 8 kg retail case reaches 14.

So the cell would bottleneck the line on most production. The fix would mean slowing the line or keeping manual backup, and either one erodes the savings further. The study needs the line's actual running rate for catering cases, and a vendor answer on whether a faster robot or gripper is available and what it costs.

## Significant issues

### 3. The safety comparison doesn't support the conclusion
- **Exposure isn't normalised.** Line 3 runs one line on one shift, which is 1 line-shift. Lines 1 and 2 run 4 line-shifts. Per line-shift, Line 3 had **4.0 injuries** against **2.75** on Lines 1 and 2. On these figures the automated line looks *worse*.
- **The products differ.** Line 3 handles 6 kg cases, while Lines 1 and 2 handle 14 kg and 8 kg cases, so the populations aren't comparable.
- **The source of injuries is unknown.** Line 3 also has an automated case packer. We don't know whether its 4 injuries or the 11 on Lines 1 and 2 relate to palletising.
- The move to single shift will roughly halve palletising exposure on Lines 1 and 2 anyway.

The safety argument may well be valid, since heavy repetitive lifting is a genuine risk. But it should rest on injury records specific to palletising, and ideally on a manual-handling risk assessment (e.g. MAC/RAPP scores). The Line 3 comparison doesn't do that job. If safety is the real justification, the study should say so openly rather than rely on a payback that doesn't hold.

### 4. Costs missing from the financial case
- Lost output during two weeks of commissioning at reduced line speed
- Reprogramming for case changeovers after the vendor's free first year
- The cost of the tighter pallet specification, likely higher pallet prices
- Technician training time and spares inventory
- Contingency, which is normally 10–15% on capital
- Energy and any civil or electrical works not in the vendor quote

### 5. The schedule is tight
A 16-week lead time from a February/March approval lands in late June or July. That leaves little slack before the August shutdown. If the shutdown is missed, the next window may fall after the single-shift change, which removes even the short two-shift benefit period.

## Minor points
- **Section 5, redeployment:** say clearly whether the savings depend on Line 5 recruitment. If the operators move to Line 5, the plant's costs don't fall unless Line 5 would otherwise hire externally.
- **Section 7, risks:** add throughput shortfall, single-shift economics, and dependence on the vendor for reprogramming.
- **Section 8:** "technically proven on our own products" overstates what the trial showed.

## Suggested way forward
1. Re-run the financials on a single-shift basis. Include sensitivity for throughput shortfall and the missing costs, and add NPV over the asset life.
2. Ask the vendor for a configuration that sustains at least 12 cases/min on the 14 kg case, or quantify the cost of running below line rate.
3. Consider alternatives that may fit single-shift economics better:
   - One cell serving both lines, or one cell on the line with the higher catering-case share
   - Lower-cost lift assists such as vacuum lifters or layer pickers for the 14 kg case
4. If safety is the main driver, present it that way with palletising-specific injury data and a risk assessment. Then ask the Board to approve on safety grounds while acknowledging the payback falls outside the hurdle.
